title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Big Picture Idea
For a given loss \ell, the regression task is

\inf_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \, \mathbb{E}[\ell(f(X), Y)],

seeking functions f with good predictive performance.
Performance depends on

Choice of loss (e.g. squared error, cross-entropy),
Choice of hypothesis class \mathcal{F} (linear models, kernels, neural networks),
Choice of regularisation (norm constraints, weight decay, spectral penalties).

Successful methods exploit inductive biases matched to data geometry. E.g. CNNs for images, GNNs for graphs, transformers for sequences, etc.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Fourier Regression
Fourier viewpoint
Any f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d) has the Fourier representation

f(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \hat f(\theta) \, e^{-i \theta^\top x} \, d\theta,

where \hat f encodes the spectral content of f. In practice, we cannot learn \hat f directly, but we can approximate f by truncating or discretising the integral:

f(x) \approx \sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j e^{-i \theta_j^\top x},

with frequencies {\theta_j} drawn either adaptively or at random. This turns regression into learning coefficients in a Fourier basis.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Fourier Regression
Why Fourier?
Fourier analysis is the harmonic analysis associated with the geometry of Euclidean space:

\mathbb{R}^d is a locally compact abelian (LCA) group under addition.
Its Haar measure is the Lebesgue measure, the unique shift-invariant measure.
By Pontryagin duality, the characters of this group are the exponentials e^{-i \theta^\top x}, and the Fourier transform is the corresponding Gelfand transform.

Thus, the Fourier basis encodes translation symmetry - the fundamental symmetry of Euclidean space.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Fourier Regression
Generalisations and Connections
There are analogous Fourier transforms on different LCA groups:

On \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} the dual group gives the Discrete Fourier Transform.
On the torus \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}, it yields the Fourier series.
On the p-adic numbers \mathbb{Q}_p, there is a corresponding Fourier transform (discussed later).
More generally, shift-invariant kernels admit a Fourier spectral representation (Bochner’s theorem). This underlies random Fourier features and spectral kernel methods.

So “Fourier regression” is not just heuristic: it’s a principled basis expansion matched to the group structure of the data, with natural regularisation in the frequency domain (e.g. penalising high frequencies).
It encodes the inductive bias of shift-invariance.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Variational Fourier Regression


How do we learn \hat{f}(\theta)?
Have been working on variational objectives: 
\mathcal{F}(Q) = \underbrace{\mathcal{L}(Q)}_{\text{Loss}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}(Q \| Q_0)}_{\text{Regulariser}},

where

▶ Q is a probability distribution
▶ Q_0 is a prior

This general objective includes: Bayesian inference, prediction centric inference, and more! Different methods:
Particle Based Methods

▶ Mean-Field Langevin Dynamics
▶ Generalisations of SVGD
▶ Fisher-Rao geometries e.g. mirror descent

Parametric Methods

▶ Normalising flows
▶ Mixtures of Gaussians (e.g. this paper)

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Issues
We might want to treat \hat f (the Fourier transform of f) as a probability measure so that we can plug it directly into the variational framework.
However:

\hat f is not generally a probability measure.

It can be complex-valued, can have negative parts, and is not normalised.
Only in special cases (e.g. positive-definite functions, characteristic functions of distributions) can \hat f be directly interpreted as a probability law.

If we force it into a probability-measure framework, then we are really heading in the direction of Bochner’s theorem: representing kernels as expectations over Fourier features.

In this case, \hat f is no longer “the Fourier transform of the predictor” but is instead treated as a spectral measure that defines a kernel.
Optimising over such spectral measures corresponds to kernel learning, not direct function learning.


Comparing with Random Fourier Features
By Bochner’s theorem: If k(x-y) is a continuous, normalised (k(0) = 1), stationary, positive-definite kernel on \mathbb{R}^d, then there exists a probability measure \lambda on \mathbb{R}^d such that

k(x,y) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i \theta^\top(x-y)} \, d\lambda(\theta).


\lambda is called the spectral measure.
If k is real-valued, \lambda must be symmetric \lambda(A)=\lambda(-A).

Random Fourier Features (RFF) approximate this integral via Monte Carlo:

k(x,y) \approx \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m \cos(\theta_j^\top(x-y)), \quad \theta_j \sim \lambda.

If you plug this approximation into Kernel Ridge Regression, the predictor has the form

f(x) = w^\top \phi(x),

where

\phi(x) = \big(\cos(\theta_1^\top x), \ldots, \cos(\theta_m^\top x)\big).


The weights w \in \mathbb{R}^m are learned by minimising the regression loss (ridge regression in this finite-dimensional feature space).
The frequencies {\theta_j} are usually fixed after the initial sampling from \lambda, though some variants learn/adapt them.

Desiderata
To create a novel approach (I think), we want to:

Treat \hat{f} as a function or signed measure
Optimise \hat{f} in an analogous framework

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Gradient flows on Riemannian Manifolds
Gradient flows in Euclidean Space
For a functional F:\mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R, the gradient flow is 
\dot x_t = -\nabla F(x_t).
 This is “steepest descent” with respect to the Euclidean inner product \langle u,v\rangle=\sum u_i v_i.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Gradient flows on Riemannian Manifolds
Generalising to a Riemannian manifold
Let (\mathcal M,g) be a Riemannian manifold:

At each point p\in\mathcal M, the tangent space T_p\mathcal M is a vector space of admissible directions.
The metric tensor g_p: T_p\mathcal M\times T_p\mathcal M\to \mathbb R is an inner product that can vary with p.

Gradient of F: the vector \nabla^g F(p)\in T_p\mathcal M such that 
dF(p)[\xi] = g_p(\nabla^g F(p), \xi) \quad\forall \xi\in T_p\mathcal M,
 where dF is the differential (directional derivative).
Gradient flow: the ODE 
\partial_t p_t = -\nabla^g F(p_t), \quad p_t\in\mathcal M.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Gradient flows on Riemannian Manifolds
Role of tangent space choice

The definition of T_p\mathcal M tells you what counts as a direction.
Example: in Wasserstein geometry, tangent vectors at a measure Q are velocity fields; in an embedding geometry, tangents are embedding perturbations.

Different tangent models give different possible evolutions.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Gradient flows on Riemannian Manifolds
Role of the metric tensor

The metric tensor tells you how to measure the size and angle of tangent vectors.
“Steepest descent” is always defined relative to this inner product.
Changing the metric changes the gradient direction.

Example:

With Euclidean metric, gradient is just \nabla F.
With a preconditioned metric g(u,v)=u^\top M v, the gradient becomes M^{-1}\nabla F.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Gradient flows on Riemannian Manifolds
Exponential map and evolution
Once you have a tangent vector v\in T_p\mathcal M, you evolve by following the geodesic starting at p with velocity v. This is the exponential map: 
p' = \exp_p(v).

So the evolution rule depends jointly on:

How you define tangents (what’s allowed),
How you measure them (the metric tensor), and
How you “integrate them back” to the manifold (the exponential map).

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
What is SVGD?
Suppose we want to optimise the objective:

\mathcal{F}(Q) = \underbrace{\mathcal{L}(Q)}_{\text{Loss}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}(Q \| Q_0)}_{\text{Regulariser}}.

A natural idea would be to consider a Riemannian manifold of probability measures and perform a gradient flow.
To recover SVGD we use the Riemannian manifold of W_2 with the tangent space given by Stein RKHS directions.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
What is SVGD?
Wasserstein W_2 Space (Otto construction)
Consider the Wasserstein-2 space: 
W_2(\mathbb{R}^d) = \left\{ P \ \text{probability measure on } \mathbb{R}^d \mid \int |x|^2 dP(x) < \infty \right\}.


Tangent space at P: 
\mathcal{T}_P W_2 = \{ -\nabla \cdot (P v) \mid v \in L^2(P;\mathbb{R}^d) \}.

Exponential map: pushing forward P by a transport map 
\exp_P(v) = (I + \varepsilon v)_\# P.

Riemannian metric: 
g_P(v,w) = \int v(x)\cdot w(x) \, dP(x).


This equips W_2 with a formal Riemannian structure (the Otto calculus).

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
What is SVGD?
Gradient Flow in W_2
Given a functional \mathcal{F}: W_2 \to \mathbb{R}, the Wasserstein gradient flow satisfies: 
\partial_t P_t = - \nabla \cdot \left(P_t \, \nabla \frac{\delta \mathcal{F}}{\delta P}(x)\right),
 where \frac{\delta \mathcal{F}}{\delta P} is the first variation of \mathcal{F}.
This is a PDE describing the evolution of measures under steepest descent in Wasserstein space.
Why not just use this?
In practice, directly solving this PDE is intractable. Instead, SVGD takes a particle approximation: 
Q \approx \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_{x_i}.

We then evolve the particles x_i along a velocity field v chosen to maximally decrease \mathcal{F}.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
What is SVGD?
Kernelised Stein Gradient
SVGD chooses v from a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) \mathcal{H}^d of vector fields with kernel k.

Stein’s identity ensures that the optimal direction of steepest descent can be expressed in closed form in this RKHS.
The resulting particle dynamics are: 
x_i \leftarrow x_i + \varepsilon \, \phi^*(x_i),
 with update function 
\phi^*(\cdot) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim Q}\big[ \nabla_x \log \pi(x) \, k(x,\cdot) + \nabla_x k(x,\cdot) \big],
 where \pi is the target distribution (often \pi \propto e^{-\mathcal{L}}).

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Option 1: Reparameterise
Rewrite our regressors as:
\begin{align*}
f(x) &= \int \hat{f}(\theta) e^{-i \theta^\top x} \,\mathrm{d}\theta \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim Q} \left[ a(\theta) e^{-i \theta^\top x}  \right].
\end{align*}
Effectively decomposes the inverse Fourier transform as:

\hat{f}(\theta) = \mathrm{d}Q(\theta) \, a(\theta).

Issues:

A vanilla approach (boring)
Need to learn a as well.
Effectively just learning a mixture distribution Q (similar to current/previous work).
The regressor just becomes a product of a(\theta) and a two-layer neural network with cosine activation (but with an interpretation as a spectral mixture).

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Option 2: Two Particle “Swarms”
Treat \hat{f} as a signed measure and use the Hahn-Jordan decomposition to write: 
\hat{f} = a\, Q^+ - b \, Q^-,
 where Q^+ and Q^- are probability measures and a,b \geq 0 are non-negative constants. To implement this:

Treat both Q^+ and Q^- as empirical measures 
Q^+ = \sum_{i=1}^m w^+_i \delta_{\theta^+_i}, \quad Q^{-} = \sum_{j = 1}^M w^-_j \delta_{\theta^-_j},

First take a step to evolve Q^+ then a step to evolve Q^- and then a vanilla Euclidean GD on (a,b) (with operator splitting).

Issues:

Nice idea but seems annoying to implement (and figure out the details)
Doubles number of hyperparameters

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Option 3: RKHS Descent
Entirely abandon forcing a probability measure and W_2. Instead, we optimise directly over a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS)!



Note: We could’ve just used L^2 instead, but an analogue of SVGD does not follow…



Let k be a PSD kernel with RKHS \mathcal{H}(k). Any signed measure \nu can be embedded in the RKHS via 
\mu_\nu(\cdot) = \int k(\theta, \cdot) \,\mathrm{d}\nu(\theta)

which induces a norm 
\| \nu \|_{\mathcal{H}(k)} = \iint k(\theta, \theta') \,\mathrm{d}\nu(\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\nu(\theta').

\mathcal{H}(k) is a Riemannian manifold with tangent space \mathcal{H}(k).
Let’s figure out the details!

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
\mathcal{L}(\nu) update derivation (can skip)

Parameter space \Theta and a PD kernel k:\Theta\times\Theta\to\mathbb R with RKHS \mathcal H_k.
For a finite signed measure \nu on \Theta, its kernel mean embedding is 
\mu_\nu(\cdot)=\int k(\cdot,\theta)\,d\nu(\theta)\in\mathcal H_k.

For a signed variation h, the corresponding embedding variation is 
\mu_h(\cdot) = \int k(\cdot,\theta)\,dh(\theta)\in\mathcal H_k.


We want to descend a functional \mathcal L(\nu). Define \tilde{\mathcal L}(\mu):=\mathcal L(\nu) with \mu=\mu_\nu.
Riemannian (RKHS) gradient
We use the Hilbert structure of \mathcal H_k. The Riemannian gradient G_\nu\in\mathcal H_k is the unique element such that 
\langle G_\nu,\mu_h\rangle_{\mathcal H_k}\;=\;D\mathcal L(\nu)[h]\quad\forall h.

This is the Riesz representation of the Fréchet derivative of \tilde{\mathcal L} at \mu_\nu.

If a pointwise functional derivative \psi_\nu exists with 
D\mathcal L(\nu)[h]=\int \psi_\nu(\theta)\,dh(\theta),
 then 
\langle G_\nu,\mu_h\rangle=\int G_\nu(\theta)\,dh(\theta)=\int \psi_\nu(\theta)\,dh(\theta),
 which implies

G_\nu=\Pi_{\mathcal H_k} \psi_\nu,
 the orthogonal projection of \psi_\nu onto \mathcal H_k.
In general, G_\nu is simply the Riesz representer; the pointwise description is optional.

Thus the gradient flow is 
\partial_t \mu_{\nu_t}=-G_{\nu_t}.

Particle form
Let \nu=\sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j \delta_{\theta_j}. Then 
\mu_\nu = \sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j k(\cdot,\theta_j).

If particles move, then (assuming k is C^1 in its second argument) 
\partial_t \mu_\nu
=\sum_j \dot\alpha_j\,k(\cdot,\theta_j)\;+\;\sum_j \alpha_j\,\nabla_{\theta_j} k(\cdot,\theta_j)\cdot \dot\theta_j.
\tag{★}

Galerkin system
Define nodal data 
g_i := G_\nu(\theta_i)=\langle G_\nu, k(\cdot,\theta_i)\rangle = D\mathcal L(\nu)[\delta_{\theta_i}].

Let 
K_{ij}=k(\theta_i,\theta_j),\qquad
B_{m:}(\theta,\alpha)=\Big[\sum_j \alpha_j \nabla_{\theta_j}k(\theta_m,\theta_j)\Big]^\top.

Projecting \partial_t\mu_\nu=-G_\nu against k(\cdot,\theta_m) gives 
K\dot\alpha+B(\theta,\alpha)\dot\theta=-g.
\tag{GS}

This expresses the orthogonal projection of the infinite-dimensional gradient onto the tangent space of the finite-dimensional particle manifold.
Choices of update

Weight-only update (exact in span). 
\boxed{\;\dot\alpha=-K^{-1}g,\quad \dot\theta=0.\;}
 This exactly matches the projected gradient using only weight changes.
Location-only update (natural gradient). Fix \dot\alpha=0 and solve least squares for \dot\theta: 
\boxed{\;\dot\theta=-(B^\top B+\lambda I)^{-1}B^\top g,\;}
 with small \lambda>0 for damping.
Joint update. Solve 
\min_{\dot\alpha,\dot\theta}\ \|K\dot\alpha+B\dot\theta+g\|_2^2
 (optionally with Tikhonov). This gives the least-squares projection of the ambient gradient.

Why approximate in \mathrm{span}\{k(\cdot,\theta_i)\}?
The manifold 
\mathcal M_m=\Big\{\sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j k(\cdot,\theta_j)\Big\}\subset\mathcal H_k
 is the finite-dimensional submanifold of the RKHS induced by m particles.
When we restrict optimisation to this manifold, we are not free to move in arbitrary directions of \mathcal H_k: the only admissible variations are those that come from perturbing the particle weights \alpha_j or their locations \theta_j.
Tangent space structure
The tangent space at \mu_\nu\in\mathcal M_m is 
T_{\mu_\nu}\mathcal M_m
=\mathrm{span}\big\{\,k(\cdot,\theta_j)\,\}_{j=1}^m \;\cup\; \{\,\nabla_{\theta_j}k(\cdot,\theta_j)\,\}_{j=1}^m.


Moving \alpha_j perturbs \mu_\nu in the direction k(\cdot,\theta_j).
Moving \theta_j perturbs \mu_\nu in the direction \nabla_{\theta_j}k(\cdot,\theta_j).

Thus the only directions available to us lie in this span.
Gradient projection
The ambient RKHS gradient G_\nu may not belong to T_{\mu_\nu}\mathcal M_m.
The correct Riemannian gradient on the submanifold is its orthogonal projection: 
\nabla^{\mathcal M_m}\mathcal L(\mu_\nu)
=\Pi_{T_{\mu_\nu}\mathcal M_m}(G_\nu).
 This is a geometric fact: gradient flows are always tangent to the manifold they evolve on.
Collocation / interpolation step
Practically, we often restrict further to the weight span \mathrm{span}\{k(\cdot,\theta_j)\}, ignoring the derivative directions.
In this case, the best approximation of G_\nu in this span is the minimum-norm kernel interpolant \hat G that matches the nodal values 
g_i := G_\nu(\theta_i).
 By standard RKHS theory (the representer/interpolation property), 
\hat G(\cdot)=\sum_{j=1}^m \beta_j k(\cdot,\theta_j),\qquad \beta=K^{-1}g,
 where K_{ij}=k(\theta_i,\theta_j).
This identity is exactly the projection of G_\nu onto the span \{k(\cdot,\theta_j)\} expressed in collocation form.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
SKL update derivation (can skip)
For sufficiently smooth vector valued \phi, can show that for T_\varepsilon = \mathrm{Id} + \varepsilon \phi: 
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \mathrm{KL}((T_\varepsilon)_\# \mu \| Q) \Big\lvert_{\varepsilon = 0} = \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim \mu}\left[ \mathcal{S}_Q \, \phi(\theta) \right],
 where 
\mathcal{S}_Q \phi =  \nabla \log q \cdot \phi + \nabla \cdot \phi
 is the vector-valued Stein operator.
Applying this to each Hahn-Jordan part of \nu and \nu_0 we have

\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \mathrm{SKL}((T_\varepsilon)_\# \nu \| \nu_0) \Big\lvert_{\varepsilon = 0} = \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim \nu^+}\left[ \mathcal{S}_{\nu_0^+} \, \phi(\theta) \right] + \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim \nu^-}\left[ \mathcal{S}_{\nu^-_0} \, \phi(\theta) \right].

For particles:

\nu = \sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j \delta_{\theta_j},

define the sign-index sets and (unnormalised) Hahn–Jordan weights 
J_+ := \{\, j : \alpha_j>0 \,\},\quad
J_- := \{\, j : \alpha_j<0 \,\},\quad
\alpha_j^{+} := \max(\alpha_j,0),\quad
\alpha_j^{-} := \max(-\alpha_j,0).

with 
w_j^{+}=\frac{\alpha_j^{+}}{\sum_{\ell\in J_+}\alpha_\ell^{+}},
\qquad
w_j^{-}=\frac{\alpha_j^{-}}{\sum_{\ell\in J_-}\alpha_\ell^{-}},
 yielding \begin{align*}
\dot{\theta}_i &= -\mathbf{1}_{\{ i\in J_+ \}}
\sum_{\ell\in J_+}\tilde w_\ell^{+}\Big(
k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell)\,\nabla \log \nu_0^{+}(\theta_\ell)
+\nabla_{\theta_\ell} k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell)
\Big) \\
&\quad -\mathbf{1}_{\{ i\in J_- \}}
\sum_{\ell\in J_-}\tilde w_\ell^{-}\Big(
k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell)\,\nabla \log \nu_0^{-}(\theta_\ell)
+\nabla_{\theta_\ell} k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell)
\Big).
\end{align*}
For an RBF kernel k(\theta,\theta')=\exp(-|\theta-\theta'|^2/(2\ell^2)), 
\nabla_{\theta_\ell}k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell)=\frac{1}{\ell^2},k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell),(\theta_i-\theta_\ell),
 so the update simplifies to 
\dot{\theta}_i
= -\sum_{\ell\in J_{\operatorname{sign}(\alpha_i)}}\tilde w_\ell^{(\operatorname{sign})}
k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell)\left[
\nabla \log \nu^{(\operatorname{sign})}(\theta_\ell)
+\frac{1}{\ell^2}(\theta_i-\theta_\ell)
\right].

text:
p-adic numbers
For a prime p, the p-adic absolute value on \mathbb{Q} is 
|x|_p=\begin{cases}
p^{-k}\, & x=p^k\frac{a}{b},\; a,b\in\mathbb{Z}, \; p\nmid a,b, \\
0,& x=0.
\end{cases}
 Numbers divisible by many powers of p are small p-adically (e.g. |8|_2=2^{-3}).
Let v_p(x)\in\mathbb{Z}\cup{\infty} be the p-adic valuation (largest k with p^k\mid x and v_p(0)=\infty). Then |x|_p=p^{-v_p(x)} and 
|x+y|_p \le \max\{|x|_p,|y|_p\}\quad\text{(ultrametric inequality).}

Completions. The completion of \mathbb{Q} under |\cdot|_p is \mathbb{Q}_p. Elements have expansions 
x=\sum_{i=k_0}^{\infty} a_i p^i, \qquad a_i\in\{0,\dots,p-1\}, \; k_0\in\mathbb{Z},
 i.e. only finitely many negative powers occur; for \mathbb{Z}_p (the compact open unit ball) we have k_0\ge 0.
Balls and measure. Closed balls are cosets a+p^m\mathbb{Z}_p. With Haar measure \mu normalised by \mu(\mathbb{Z}_p)=1, one has \mu(a+p^m\mathbb{Z}_p)=p^{-m}.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Hierarchical data and p-adics
The ultrametric induces a tree: each ball a+p^m\mathbb{Z}_p splits into p disjoint children a+bp^m+p^{m+1}\mathbb{Z}_p, b\in{0,\dots,p-1}. Two points are close iff they agree to many leading base-p digits: 
v_p(x-y)=\text{length of the longest common prefix of the $p$-adic digit strings of $x,y$.}

Canonical encodings.

Binary/quad strings (e.g. taxonomy, DNA): choose p=2 or p=4. Encode a finite string s=(s_0,\dots,s_{L-1}) as x=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1} s_i p^i\in\mathbb{Z}_p. Then 
v_p(x-x')=\min{i: s_i\neq s_i'}\quad(\text{or } \infty \text{ if identical}),
 so distance equals first divergence depth in the tree.
General rooted trees of out-degree \le p: label edges 0,\dots,p-1 from root and encode the path label as above.

This makes \mathbb{Q}_p a natural host for clustering, phylogenies, and any prefix-based similarity.

Gelfand transform (p-adic Fourier analysis)
Consider the LCA group (\mathbb{Q}_p,+) with Haar measure \mu (\mu(\mathbb{Z}_p)=1). Fix the standard additive character \psi:\mathbb{Q}_p\to\mathbb{T} that is trivial on \mathbb{Z}_p and non-trivial on p^{-1}\mathbb{Z}_p (concretely, \psi(x)=e^{2\pi i {x}_p}, where {x}_p\in\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z} is determined by the finitely many negative-power digits of x).

Fourier/Gelfand transform: 
\widehat{f}(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{Q}_p} f(x)\,\psi(\xi x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad \xi\in\mathbb{Q}_p.

Inversion/Plancherel (with dual Haar d\xi): 
f(x)=\int_{\mathbb{Q}_p} \widehat{f}(\xi)\,\psi(-\xi x)\,d\xi\,\qquad |f|_2=|\widehat f|_2.

Characters. Every continuous character is \chi_\xi(x)=\psi(\xi x) for a unique \xi\in\mathbb{Q}_p; the dual group is \widehat{\mathbb{Q}}_p\cong\mathbb{Q}_p.

Practical evaluation. If computations are at resolution m (finite strings/digits), then 
\chi_\xi(x)=\exp\Big(2\pi i \;\frac{(\xi x)\bmod p^m}{p^m}\Big),
 so you only need modular arithmetic on integers of size p^m.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
How to generalise SVGD
Standard SVGD and the Langevin Stein operator
SVGD is built on the observation that the gradient flow of a variational objective between a particle approximation Q and the target \pi can be expressed through a Stein operator.
In the standard setting, SVGD uses the Langevin Stein operator, which arises from the infinitesimal generator of the Langevin diffusion:

\mathrm{d}X_t = \tfrac{1}{2}\nabla \log \pi(X_t)\,\mathrm{d}t + \mathrm{d}W_t.

This diffusion leaves \pi invariant. Its generator \mathcal{A} acts on smooth test functions f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R} by

(\mathcal{A}f)(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}\nabla \log \pi(x)^\top \nabla f(x) + \tfrac{1}{2}\Delta f(x).

The Stein operator is then defined as \mathcal{S}_\pi f = \mathcal{A}f. By reversibility of the diffusion w.r.t. \pi,

\mathbb{E}_{X\sim \pi}[(\mathcal{S}_\pi f)(X)] = 0,

which is the Stein identity. SVGD then searches for the steepest descent direction in an RKHS defined by a kernel k, leading to the update

\phi^*(z) = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim Q}\left[\,\nabla_x \log \pi(x)\,k(z,x) + \nabla_x k(z,x)\,\right].

Stein operators from Markov kernels
The Langevin diffusion is only one possible Markov process with invariant law \pi. In fact, any Markov kernel P that leaves \pi invariant can be used to define a valid Stein operator:

(\mathcal{S}_\pi f)(x) := (P f)(x) - f(x),

because stationarity gives

\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[(\mathcal{S}_\pi f)(X)] = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[Pf(X)] - \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[f(X)] = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[f(X)] - \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[f(X)] = 0.

This form is the discrete-time analogue of the Langevin generator.

If P is a small-step Euler–Maruyama discretisation of Langevin, then (Pf-f)/\delta t \to \mathcal{A}f.
If P is a Metropolis–Hastings kernel, the operator encodes both proposals and accept/reject.
If P is Hamiltonian dynamics, the operator encodes HMC.

Thus, SVGD can be viewed as one instance of a general recipe: pick any \pi-invariant kernel P, form its Stein operator, and use this to construct an RKHS descent direction.
What changes when replacing Langevin with a general P?
The steepest descent field now becomes

\phi^*(z) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{x\sim q}\big[ (P k)(z,x) - k(z,x)\big],

where (Pk)(z,x) := \mathbb{E}_{x'\sim P(\cdot|x)}[,k(z,x')\,].

For Langevin, (Pk)(z,x) reduces (in the \delta t \to 0 limit) to terms involving \nabla_x\log \pi(x) and \nabla_x k(z,x).
For MH, it involves an expectation over proposals and accept/rejects, which can be estimated by Monte Carlo.
For HMC, it involves simulating a Hamiltonian trajectory and averaging kernel evaluations.

The result is an SVGD-like update that inherits the structure of the chosen MCMC kernel. We can think of this as a Steinised MCMC scheme: each particle update is guided by the kernelised Stein operator of P, while (depending on the MCMC sheme/choice) retainin an MH correction to ensure correctness.
Issues with Langevin-only SVGD
Why go beyond Langevin?

Autocorrelation and mixing: Standard SVGD uses only local Langevin gradients; it may explore poorly in multimodal targets.
Accept/reject structure: Langevin has no accept/reject, so SVGD inherits its bias.
Rigid operator choice: The Langevin generator enforces a gradient form; other MCMC kernels encode richer moves (e.g. Hamiltonian trajectories, independence proposals).
Differentiable Structure: The use of Langevin generator assumes a gradient can be computed - not the case for \mathbb{Q}_p spaces.

By generalising SVGD to arbitrary \pi-invariant kernels, we can:

Design particle-based samplers that retain MH corrections (hence exactness).
Incorporate repulsive Stein interactions directly into MCMC updates, reducing the need for post-processing (like Stein thinning).
Leverage richer dynamics (HMC, independence MH, etc.) while still benefiting from the RKHS optimisation framework.

Aside: Continuous Time Markov Processes and Stein Operators
Continuos Time Markov Processes
If \pi is stationary for a continuous-time Markov process (X_t) with semigroup (P_t)_{t\geq 0}, then for every t\ge 0:

\pi P_t = \pi,

i.e. 
\int (P_t f)(x)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x) = \int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x), \qquad \forall f.

So P_t preserves expectations under \pi.
The generator is defineds as

\mathcal{A} f = \lim_{t\to 0^+} \frac{P_t f - f}{t}.

Stein Operator
A Stein operator \mathcal{S}_\pi is an operator such that \mathbb{E}_{X\sim \pi}[\mathcal{S}_\pi f(X)]=0 for all f in its Stein class.
The natural way to construct a Stein operator is via semigroups or generators for a \pi invariant Markov process (or discrete time analogues).

Semigroup: Define \mathcal{S}_t f := P_t f - f, with (P_t)_{t\geq 0} a \pi invariant semigroup. Then 
  \mathbb{E}_\pi[\mathcal{S}_t f] = \int (P_t f - f) \, d\pi = 0,
  
Generator: Define \mathcal{S}_\pi := \mathcal{A} with \mathcal{A} a \pi invariant generator, then 
\mathbb{E}_\pi[\mathcal{S}_\pi f] = \mathbb{E}_\pi[\mathcal{A} f] = \mathbb{E}_\pi\left[\lim_{t\to 0^+} \frac{P_t f - f}{t}\right] = 0.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Introduction to SVGD
Let \pi be a target density on \mathbb{R}^d and Q a current approximation. The KL divergence is:

\mathrm{KL}(Q \| \pi) = \int \log\left(\frac{dQ}{d\pi}\right) \,\mathrm{d}Q.

Consider the infinitesimal transport T_\varepsilon(x)=x+\varepsilon\,\phi(x) with a vector field \phi:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d. We choose \phi to maximise the instantaneous decrease of KL:

\min_{\phi}\ \left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \mathrm{KL}\big((T_\varepsilon)_\# Q \| \pi\big)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}.

By a calculation involving change of variables and a Taylor series expansion of the density of (T_\varepsilon)_\# Q, it can be shown:

\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \left.\mathrm{KL}( (T_\varepsilon)_\# Q \| \pi  )\right|_{\varepsilon = 0} = -\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}\left[ (\mathcal{A}_\pi \phi)(X) \right],

where \mathcal{A}_\pi \phi = \phi^\top \nabla \log \pi  + \nabla\cdot\phi.
Now restrict \phi to the vector-valued RKHS 
\mathcal H_K = \bigoplus_{i=1}^d \mathcal H_k,
\qquad K(z,x)=k(z,x)\,I_d,
 where k:\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R} is a scalar positive-definite kernel and I_d is the d\times d identity. Using the reproducing properties in \mathcal H_K, the functional \phi \mapsto \mathbb{E}_Q[\mathcal{A}_\pi \phi] has Riesz representer 
\boxed{\;
\Phi_Q(z) = \mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}\left[k(z,X)\nabla\log\pi(X) + \nabla_X k(z,X)\right].
\;}
 where \nabla_X k(z,X) denotes the gradient of k w.r.t. its second argument.
Then, since \mathcal{H}_K is a Hilbert space, Cauchy-Schwarz tells us:

-\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \left.\mathrm{KL}( (T_\varepsilon)_\# Q \| \pi  )\right|_{\varepsilon = 0} = \mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}\left[ (\mathcal{A}_\pi \phi)(X) \right] = \langle \phi, \Phi_Q \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_K} \leq \|\phi\|_{\mathcal{H}_K} \|\Phi_Q\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}.

We wish to maximise this. Therefore, the steepest descent direction over the unit ball is \phi^* = \tfrac{\Phi_Q}{\|\Phi_Q\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}}. In practice we use the field 
\boxed{\;\phi_{\text{SVGD}}(z) = \Phi_Q(z)
=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}\left[k(z,X)\nabla\log\pi(X) + \nabla_X k(z,X)\right].}

A single Euler step updates particles x_i\leftarrow x_i+\eta\,\phi_{\text{SVGD}}(x_i). Moreover, 
\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\ \mathrm{KL}\big((T_\varepsilon)_\# Q  \| \pi\big) \right|_{\varepsilon = 0}
= -\|\Phi_Q\|_{\mathcal H_K}^2,
 i.e. the squared kernel Stein discrepancy (KSD) equals the instantaneous KL decrease along \phi_{\text{SVGD}}.
Empirical form: With particles \{x_j\}_{j=1}^n defining an empirical measure Q = \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \delta_{x_j}, the SVGD update becomes: 
\phi_{\text{SVGD}}(z) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \Big[k(z,x_j)\,\nabla\log\pi(x_j) + \nabla_{x_j} k(z,x_j)\Big].

text:
Big picture
Goal: Generate high-quality (ideally independent) samples from a target density \pi.
Standard Approaches:

MCMC produces asymptotically exact samples but with autocorrelation; thinning/post-processing is usually required.
SVGD (Stein Variational Gradient Descent) gives deterministic, interacting particles with built-in repulsion, but needs a differentiable score \nabla\log\pi and often struggles on multimodal targets.

Idea: For any \pi-invariant Markov kernel P (or generator \mathcal{A}) we:

take its Stein operator T_\pi,
build the Stein RKHS geometry induced by a kernel k,
construct an analogue of SVGD

This yields a generalised SVGD whose update is a “particle version” of the given MCMC—preserving invariance while adding SVGD style repulsion. With Metropolis–Hastings (MH), you get a Stein-tilted MH step that remains \pi-invariant but encourages diversity.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Alternative View of Vanilla SVGD
It turns out, you can derive the “vanilla” SVGD updates by using a different objective!
Ingredients

Target: Density \pi on \mathbb R^d.
Feature operator: \mathcal G_\pi f=\nabla f+f\, \nabla \log \pi (scalar \to vector).
Divergence Stein operator: (\mathcal S_\pi\phi)=\nabla\cdot\phi+\phi\cdot \nabla \log \pi (vector \to scalar).
Scalar base kernel: k: \mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d\rightarrow\mathbb{R}.

Matrix Stein Kernel and its RKHS
Using the feature operator \mathcal{G}_\pi, define the matrix stein kernel: 
K_{\mathcal G_\pi}(z,x) = \big(\nabla_z+\nabla \log \pi(z)\big)\big(\nabla_x+\nabla \log \pi(x)\big)^{\top}k(z,x)\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}.

Its RKHS \mathcal H_{K_{\mathcal G_\pi}} consists of vector-valued functions with reproducing rule

\big\langle \phi,\ K_{\mathcal G_\pi}(\cdot,x)v\big\rangle_{\mathcal H}
= v^{\top}(\mathcal S_\pi\phi)(x)\qquad(\forall\,\phi\in\mathcal H,\,v\in\mathbb R^d).
\tag{R}

Defining \Phi_Q
As in the previous derivation, we define: 
\Phi_Q(z) = \mathbb E_{X\sim Q}\!\big[k(z,X)(\nabla \log \pi(X)+\nabla_X k(z,X))\big] = \mathbb E_{X\sim Q}\!\big[K_{\mathcal G_\pi}(z,X)\mathbf 1\big]

By (R), 
\boxed{\;\langle \phi,\Phi_Q\rangle_{\mathcal H}
=\mathbb E_{X\sim Q}\big[(\mathcal S_\pi \phi)(X)\big]\quad(\forall\,\phi\in\mathcal H).\;}
\tag{*}

KSD and the objective. 
\mathrm{KSD}(Q|\pi)=|\Phi_Q|_{\mathcal H},
\qquad
J(Q)=\tfrac12|\Phi_Q|_{\mathcal H}^2.

Goal
Show that the Gâteaux derivative of J along a transport Q_\varepsilon=(\mathrm{Id}+\varepsilon\phi)_\# Q with direction \phi\in\mathcal H is 
\boxed{\;\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{0}J(Q_\varepsilon)=\langle \phi,\ \Phi_Q\rangle_{\mathcal H}.\;}
\tag{G}
 Hence the steepest descent over |\phi|_{\mathcal H}\le 1 is \phi^\star=-\Phi_Q/|\Phi_Q|, and using \phi=-\Phi_Q yields the SVGD field.
Derivation
We proceed entirely inside the Stein RKHS (\mathcal H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathcal H}).
Step 1 — Differentiate J(Q_\varepsilon) via \Phi_{Q_\varepsilon}.
Since J(Q)=\tfrac12\langle \Phi_Q,\Phi_Q\rangle_{\mathcal H}, 
\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{0}J(Q_\varepsilon)
=\big\langle \Phi_Q,\ \dot\Phi_Q\big\rangle_{\mathcal H},
\qquad \dot\Phi_Q:=\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{0}\Phi_{Q_\varepsilon}\in\mathcal H.
\tag{1}

To identify \dot\Phi_Q, use only the reproducing identity (*).
Step 2 — Characterise \dot\Phi_Q by testing against \psi\in\mathcal H.
For any \psi\in\mathcal H, 
\langle \psi,\ \Phi_{Q_\varepsilon}\rangle_{\mathcal H}
=\mathbb E_{X\sim Q_\varepsilon}\big[(\mathcal S_\pi\psi)(X)\big].
 Differentiate at \varepsilon=0. The pushforward path Q_\varepsilon=(\mathrm{Id}+\varepsilon\phi)_\# Q satisfies the continuity equation at \varepsilon=0: \partial_\varepsilon q_\varepsilon|_{0}=-\nabla\cdot(q\phi). Hence for any smooth test h, 
\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{0}\mathbb E_{Q_\varepsilon}[h]
= \int h\,\partial_\varepsilon q_\varepsilon\Big|_{0}
= -\int h\,\nabla\cdot(q\phi)
= \int q\,\nabla h\cdot \phi
= \mathbb E_Q[\nabla h\cdot \phi].
 Apply this with h=\mathcal S_\pi\psi (a scalar): 
\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{0}
\langle \psi,\ \Phi_{Q_\varepsilon}\rangle_{\mathcal H}
= \mathbb E_Q\!\big[\nabla(\mathcal S_\pi\psi)(X)\cdot \phi(X)\big].
\tag{2}

On the other hand, 
\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{0}
\langle \psi,\ \Phi_{Q_\varepsilon}\rangle_{\mathcal H}
= \langle \psi,\ \dot\Phi_Q\rangle_{\mathcal H}.
\tag{3}

Thus \dot\Phi_Q\in\mathcal H is the unique element satisfying, for all \psi\in\mathcal H, 
\boxed{\;\langle \psi,\ \dot\Phi_Q\rangle_{\mathcal H}
= \mathbb E_Q\!\big[\nabla(\mathcal S_\pi\psi)\cdot \phi\big].\;}
\tag{4}

Step 3 — Identify the directional derivative of J.
Set \psi=\Phi_Q in (4) and use (1): 
\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{0}J(Q_\varepsilon)
= \langle \Phi_Q,\ \dot\Phi_Q\rangle_{\mathcal H}
= \mathbb E_Q\!\big[\nabla(\mathcal S_\pi\Phi_Q)\cdot \phi\big].
\tag{5}

Now invoke the Stein reproducing property (R) with the specific kernel K_{\mathcal G_\pi}: by construction of \mathcal H one has the identity 
\boxed{\;\mathbb E_Q\!\big[\nabla(\mathcal S_\pi\psi)\cdot \phi\big]
= \langle \phi,\ \psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}\qquad(\forall\,\phi,\psi\in\mathcal H),\;}
\tag{IP}
 which is the RKHS version of integration by parts generated by K_{\mathcal G_\pi}. Applying (IP) with \psi=\Phi_Q yields 
\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{0}J(Q_\varepsilon)
= \langle \phi,\ \Phi_Q\rangle_{\mathcal H}.
 This is exactly (G).
(Sketch justification of (IP): write \phi=\sum_m K_{\mathcal G_\pi}(\cdot,x_m)v_m (or the Bochner integral analogue); then \mathcal S_\pi\psi pairs with K_{\mathcal G_\pi} via (R), and differentiating under the integral evaluates the \nabla-action, yielding \langle \phi,\psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}.)
Step 4 — Steepest descent and the SVGD field
By Cauchy–Schwarz in \mathcal H, 
\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{0}J(Q_\varepsilon)
= \langle \phi,\ \Phi_Q\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\;\ge\; -\,|\phi|_{\mathcal H}\,|\Phi_Q|_{\mathcal H}.
 Over the unit ball \{\phi:|\phi|_{\mathcal H}\le 1\}, the minimiser is 
\boxed{\;\phi^\star=-\frac{\Phi_Q}{|\Phi_Q|_{\mathcal H}};}
 (and in practice one uses \phi=-\Phi_Q with a stepsize). Expanding \Phi_Q gives the familiar SVGD field 
\phi_{\text{SVGD}}(z)
= -\,\mathbb E_{X\sim Q}\big[k(z,X)(\nabla \log \pi(X)+\nabla_X k(z,X))\big].

Thus the gradient flow of J=\tfrac12\mathrm{KSD}^2 in the Stein RKHS geometry coincides with SVGD.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Aside: Stein Operators
A Stein operator for a target \pi is any operator T_\pi such that

\mathbb{E}_{X\sim \pi}[ (T_\pi f)(X)] = 0.

There are three kinds of “Stein” operators which can make things confusing:

Generators on scalars: An operator \mathcal{A}_\pi which takes in scalar-valued functions and outputs scalar-valued functions.

\mathcal{A}_\pi f = \nabla \cdot \nabla f + \nabla\log\pi \cdot \nabla f

Vector to scalar: An operator \mathcal{S}_\pi which takes in vector-valued functions and outputs scalar-valued functions. 
\mathcal{S}_\pi \phi = \nabla \cdot \phi + \nabla\log\pi \cdot \phi.

Scalar to vector (Stein feature operator): An operator \mathcal{G}_\pi which takes in scalar-valued functions and outputs vector valued functions. 
\mathcal{G}_\pi f = \nabla f + f \, \nabla \log \pi.


They are related:

\mathcal{A}_\pi f = \mathcal{S}_\pi (\nabla f) = \nabla \cdot (\mathcal{G}_\pi f).

Creating Stein Operators
A natural way to construct a Stein operator is through Markov processes which leave the target \pi invariant.
Discrete Time
For a discrete time \pi-invariant Markov process with Markov kernel P, we can define the Markov-Stein operator associated with P:

(T_\pi f)(x) \coloneqq (P f)(x)-f(x).

It satisfies the Stein identity \mathbb E_\pi[T_\pi f]=0 for bounded measurable f since \pi P = \pi and \int P f\,\mathrm{d}\pi = \int f\,\mathrm{d}\pi.
Continuous Time
In a continuous time \pi-invariant Markov process, we can construct a Stein operator via the semigroup or its generator:

Semigroup: Define \mathcal{S}_t f := P_t f - f, with (P_t)_{t\geq 0} a \pi invariant semigroup. Then 
  \mathbb{E}_\pi[\mathcal{S}_t f] = \int (P_t f - f) \, d\pi = 0,
  
Generator: Define \mathcal{S}_\pi := \mathcal{A} with \mathcal{A} a \pi invariant generator, then 
\mathbb{E}_\pi[\mathcal{S}_\pi f] = \mathbb{E}_\pi[\mathcal{A} f] = \mathbb{E}_\pi\left[\lim_{t\to 0^+} \frac{P_t f - f}{t}\right] = 0.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
The Generalisation (discrete time)
Ingredients

Target: \pi.
A \pi-invariant Markov kernel P (discrete-time), i.e. 
\int \pi(dx)\,P(x,dy)=\pi(dy)

The Markov–Stein operator associated with P: 
(T_\pi f)(x) \coloneqq (P f)(x)-f(x).
 It satisfies the Stein identity \mathbb E_\pi[T_\pi f]=0 for a broad class of f.

We consider a family of \pi-invariant kernels \{M_\varepsilon:\varepsilon\in(-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)\} with M_0=P. Think of 
X_0\sim q,\qquad X_1\mid X_0\sim M_\varepsilon(X_0,\cdot),
 so the one-step update maps q to q M_\varepsilon.
“Admissible direction”
We say that \{M_\varepsilon\} realises an admissible direction \varphi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R at \varepsilon=0 if, for every sufficiently smooth/bounded test function f, 
\left. \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \mathbb E_{X_0\sim q,\ X_1\sim M_\varepsilon(X_0,\cdot)}\big[f(X_1)\big] \right|_{\varepsilon = 0} = \mathbb E_{X_0\sim q}\big[(T_\pi f)(X_0) \varphi(X_0)\big].

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
The Generalisation
In vanilla SVGD, the “Stein field” was 
\phi_{\text{SVGD}}(z)
=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}\left[k(z,X)\nabla\log\pi(X) + \nabla_X k(z,X)\right] = \mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\mathcal{G}_\pi^X k(z,X)],
 where (\mathcal{G}_\pi) f(x) = f(x) \nabla\log\pi(x) + \nabla f(x) is the scalar \to vector Stein feature operator.
For a Markov-Stein operator \mathcal{S}_P f = Pf - f, this implies we want something like:

\phi_{P\text{-SVGD}}(z) = \mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\mathcal{S}_P^X k(z,X)].

Issues

As written, the \phi_{P\text{-SVGD}}(z) is not a transport map - it is scalar-valued!
Even if it did make sense, how can it be justified?
The derivation of the standard SVGD assumed the use of KL divergence and transports of the form 
T_\varepsilon = \mathrm{Id} + \varepsilon\,\phi.

With these assumptions, the Langevin Stein operator \mathcal{S}_\pi appeared.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Alternative View
Instead of considering a transport map to move Q, we consider a family of Markov kernels:

\{ P_{\varepsilon} \mid -\epsilon_0 \leq \varepsilon \leq \epsilon_0, \; P_0 = P \}.

Define

F(\varepsilon) = \mathrm{KL}(Q \, P_\varepsilon \| \pi ).

We seek the Markov kernel which maximises the instaneous decrease of KL:

F'(0) = \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \left. \mathrm{KL}(Q \, P_\varepsilon \| \pi ) \right|_{\varepsilon = 0}.

Constraints on P_\varepsilon
Let (P_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon} be a family of Markov kernels with P_0=P. For bounded measurable f, write 
(P_\varepsilon f)(x)=\int f(y)\,P_\varepsilon(x,dy).
 If the map \varepsilon\mapsto P_\varepsilon f is differentiable at 0 for all bounded f, define the signed kernel derivative M by 
(M f)(x)\;:=\;\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\,(P_\varepsilon f)(x)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}.
 By Riesz–Markov, this means that for each fixed x, there exists a finite signed measure M(x,\cdot) on the state space so that 
(M f)(x)=\int f(y)\,M(x,dy).

Intuitively: P_\varepsilon = P + \varepsilon M + o(\varepsilon) in the weak sense.
Now differentiate the standard identities:
Stochasticity (row sums =1).
For every \varepsilon and x, \int P_\varepsilon(x,dy)=1. Differentiate at 0: 
\int M(x,dy)=0\quad\text{for all }x
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
M\, 1 =0.

\pi-invariance to first order.
If P_\varepsilon leaves \pi invariant for all \varepsilon, then for every bounded f, 
\int (P_\varepsilon f)(x)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x)=\int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x).
 Differentiate at 0: 
\int (M f)(x)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x)=0\quad\text{for all }f.
 Equivalently, as a signed measure in y, 
\int M(x,dy)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x)=0
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\pi M=0.

Reversibility (detailed balance) to first order.
If each P_\varepsilon is \pi-reversible, then for all measurable sets A,B: 
\int_A\!\!\int_B \mathrm{d}\pi(x)\,P_\varepsilon(x,dy)
=
\int_A\!\!\int_B \pi(dy)\,P_\varepsilon(y,dx).
 Differentiate at 0 and use symmetry in (A,B) to get, as measures on \mathcal X\times\mathcal X, 
\pi(dx)\,M(x,dy)\;=\;\pi(dy)\,M(y,dx).
 This is the “detailed balance at first order”.
Parameterising P_\varepsilon
Assume P is \pi-reversible and set 
\mu(dx,dy):=\pi(dx)\,P(x,dy).
 Then \mu is symmetric: \mu(dx,dy)=\mu(dy,dx).
A class of perturbations is obtained by weighting the jump x\to y with a function A(x,y) and compensating on the diagonal so rows still sum to zero: 
(Mf)(x)=\int\big(f(y)-f(x)\big)\,A(x,y)\,P(x,dy).
 Equivalently, as (signed) kernels, 
M(x,dy)=A(x,y)\,P(x,dy)\;-\;\Big[\int A(x,z)\,P(x,dz)\Big]\,\delta_x(dy).
\tag{†}

Let’s check the three constraints and see what symmetry of A is forced:
Row sums. With f\equiv 1, (Mf)(x)=\int(1-1)\,A(\cdot)\,P=0. So M\mathbf 1=0 holds for any A.
\pi-invariance at first order. For any f, 
\int (Mf)(x)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x)=\iint \big(f(y)-f(x)\big)\,A(x,y)\,\mu(dx,dy).
 Swap (x,y) and use symmetry of \mu to see this integral is the negative of itself, hence 0 regardless of the symmetry of A. Thus \pi M=0 always holds.
Reversibility at first order. Here the symmetry of A matters. From (†), 
\pi(dx)\,M(x,dy)=A(x,y)\,\mu(dx,dy)\;-\;\pi(dx)\,a(x)\,\delta_x(dy),
\qquad a(x):=\int A(x,z)\,P(x,dz).
 Swapping (x,y) we obtain \pi(dy)\,M(y,dx)=A(y,x)\,\mu(dx,dy)-\pi(dy)\,a(y)\,\delta_y(dx). For these two signed measures to be equal, we must have on the off-diagonal (where \delta-terms vanish) 
A(x,y)\,\mu(dx,dy)=A(y,x)\,\mu(dx,dy)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
A(x,y)=A(y,x)\quad(\mu\text{-a.e.}).
 The diagonal compensation terms then match automatically.
Conclusion: to preserve reversibility to first order, A must be symmetric \mu-a.e.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Derivation
Step 1: Gâteaux derivative of \mathrm{KL}
Let Q\ll \pi with density \rho=\dfrac{dQ}{d\pi} and 
\mathrm{KL}(Q\|\pi)=\int \rho\log\rho\,d\pi.
 Consider a differentiable path of probability measures (Q_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon} with Q_0=Q and 
\dot Q := \left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} Q_\varepsilon \right|_{\varepsilon=0},
\qquad \dot Q(\mathcal X)=0.
 Assume Q_\varepsilon\ll\pi for |\varepsilon| small with densities \rho_\varepsilon=\dfrac{dQ_\varepsilon}{d\pi} differentiable at \varepsilon=0 \pi-a.e., and \dot\rho:=\left.\dfrac{d}{d\varepsilon}\rho_\varepsilon \right|_{\varepsilon=0}. Then d\dot q=\dot\rho\,d\pi.
Write \varphi(t)=t\log t. Then \varphi'(t)=1+\log t and 
F(\varepsilon):=\mathrm{KL}(Q_\varepsilon\|\pi)=\int \varphi(\rho_\varepsilon)\,d\pi.
 By differentiation under the integral sign: 
F'(0)=\int \varphi'(\rho)\,\dot\rho\,d\pi
=\int \bigl(1+\log\rho\bigr)\,d\dot Q.
 Because \dot Q(\mathcal X)=\int 1\,d\dot Q=0, the constant “1” drops out: 
F'(0)=\int \log\rho\,d\dot Q
=\int \log\!\Big(\frac{dQ}{d\pi}\Big)\,d\dot Q.

Step 2: What is the allowable \dot q?
Given a current law Q, the one–step pushforward along P_\varepsilon is Q_\varepsilon:=Q\,P_\varepsilon. Its tangent is 
\dot Q
:=\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\, Q\,P_\varepsilon\right|_{\varepsilon=0}
= QM,
\qquad\text{i.e.}\quad
\langle f,\dot Q\rangle
=\int (Mf)(x)\,Q(dx).

Using the property of M: 
\boxed{\;
\langle f,\dot q\rangle
=\iint \big(f(y)-f(x)\big)\,A(x,y)\,\underbrace{q(dx)\,P(x,dy)}_{=:~\mu_Q(dx,dy)}\;.
}
\tag{Tangent}
 Here \mu_q is the one–step coupling of (Q,P). Note \mu_q is generally not symmetric unless Q=\pi.
Step 3: First variation of \mathrm{KL}
The Gâteaux derivative of KL gives 
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\left.\mathrm{KL}(Q\,P_\varepsilon\|\pi) \right|_{\varepsilon=0}
=\int \log\!\Big(\frac{dQ}{d\pi}\Big)\,d\dot Q
=\left\langle \log\dfrac{dQ}{d\pi},\dot Q\right\rangle.
 Therefore: 
\boxed{\;
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\Big|_{\varepsilon=0}\mathrm{KL}(Q\,P_\varepsilon\|\pi)
= \iint \big(\log\dfrac{dQ}{d\pi}(y)-\log\dfrac{dQ}{d\pi}(x)\big)\,A(x,y)\,\mu_Q(dx,dy)\;.
}

This is the general first–order formula for any admissible perturbation (i.e. any symmetric A in (\dagger)).

title: Variational Fourier Regression
section: Step 2: What is the allowable \dot q?
text:
Step 2: What is the allowable \dot q?
Given a current law q, the one–step pushforward along P_\varepsilon is q_\varepsilon:=qP_\varepsilon. Its tangent is 
\dot q
:=\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\, qP_\varepsilon\right|_{0}
= qM,
\qquad\text{i.e.}\quad
\langle f,\dot q\rangle
=\int (Mf)(x)\,q(dx).

Using (\dagger), 
\boxed{\;
\langle f,\dot q\rangle
=\iint \big(f(y)-f(x)\big)\,A(x,y)\,\underbrace{q(dx)\,P(x,dy)}_{=:~\mu_q(dx,dy)}\;.
}
\tag{Tangent}
 Here \mu_q is the one–step coupling of (q,P). Note \mu_q is generally not symmetric unless q=\pi.
Step 3: First variation of \mathrm{KL}
Let \rho=\dfrac{dq}{d\pi} and \ell:=\log\rho. The standard Gâteaux derivative of KL gives 
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\Big|_{0}\mathrm{KL}(qP_\varepsilon\|\pi)
=\int \log\!\Big(\frac{dq}{d\pi}\Big)\,d\dot q
=\langle \ell,\dot q\rangle.
 Insert (()) with f=\ell: 
\boxed{\;
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\Big|_{0}\mathrm{KL}(qP_\varepsilon\|\pi)
= \iint \big(\ell(y)-\ell(x)\big)\,A(x,y)\,\mu_q(dx,dy)\;.
}
\tag{KL-Var}

This is the general first–order formula for any admissible perturbation (i.e. any symmetric A in (\dagger)).
Two illuminating rewrites:

Symmetrised form. Split \mu_q into its symmetric and anti-symmetric parts: 
\mu_q^s:=\tfrac12(\mu_q+\mu_q^\top),\quad
\mu_q^a:=\tfrac12(\mu_q-\mu_q^\top),
 with \mu_q^\top(dy,dx):=\mu_q(dx,dy). Since A is symmetric, only \mu_q^a contributes: 
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\Big|_{0}\mathrm{KL}
= 2\iint \big(\ell(y)-\ell(x)\big)\,A(x,y)\,\mu_q^a(dx,dy).
 In particular, if q=\pi (hence \mu_q=\mu symmetric), the derivative is 0, as it must be.
Dirichlet cross-term (if q is close to \pi). When q is near \pi, the antisymmetric part is small and one can replace \mu_q by \mu at leading order, obtaining the familiar symmetric bilinear form 
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\Big|_{0}\mathrm{KL}
\approx
\tfrac12\iint \big(\ell(y)-\ell(x)\big)\,\big(\underbrace{2A(x,y)}_{\text{symmetric}}\big)\,\mu(dx,dy).
